raw_response:
I have been farming these lands for 35 years. I am 74 now, and my body is not what it used to be—my knees ache when I squat for too long, and bending to pick cotton wears me out. But I know every corner of my 5 mu. My household has only two people, and my family member works off-farm in the city, sending back some money. That helps, but I still need to grow my own food and earn cash from the land. I rely on my well for water, so I am not afraid of dry spells.

This year, I will plant **2 mu of cotton** and **3 mu of spring maize**. Cotton brings good cash, but it is backbreaking work—picking, pruning, and spraying again and again. At my age, 2 mu is all I can manage by myself. The remaining 3 mu will go to spring maize. Maize is easier to look after, gives us grain to eat and sell, and does not need as much bending and hand labor.

I will buy **hybrid seeds** from the village supply shop, the same kinds my neighbors use. I cannot read the packages, but I recognize the bags by color, and the shopkeeper knows I need the ones that grow well here.

For fertilizer, I will spread **compound fertilizer** as a basal dose before planting. For cotton, I will apply a bit more potash because it helps the bolls. For maize, I will put down a standard dose and maybe top-dress with a little urea when the plants are knee-high if they look hungry. I have learned over the years that putting too much fertilizer wastes money and can burn the crop.

With my well, I will irrigate **three times for cotton**—at flowering, at boll-setting, and once more if the autumn is dry. For maize, **two times** is usually enough: once at the jointing stage and once at tasseling. I flood the furrows as I have always done.

Cotton always suffers from bollworms and aphids, so I must spray **many times**—about **12 applications** in total, mixing insecticide, herbicide, and sometimes plant growth regulator. For maize, I only need **3 sprays**: one for weeds and one or two for insects when the armyworms appear.

I will **rotary till** all the plots before sowing. No-tillage might save fuel, but I like to turn the soil and break up the stubble from last year. It makes me feel the land is clean and ready.

If the weather treats me fairly and no big disaster comes, I expect my cotton to yield around **500 kg per mu** of seed cotton, and my maize to yield about **950 kg per mu**. These are honest numbers based on what this land usually gives me.
